Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Review safe surgical technique for ankle arthroplasty, including patient setup, instrumentation,
and portal placement.
Anterior Ankle Arthroscopy
Overview
Thorough knowledge of the surface anatomy of the foot and ankle is required to perform safe,
successful ankle arthroscopy.
Good working knowledge of the interrelationships between the bony landmarks and the
tendons, arteries, veins, and the superficial and deep nerves of the ankle is necessary.
The workhorse portals for anterior ankle arthroscopy are the anteromedial, the anterolateral,
and the optional posterolateral portals1 (Video 1).

Figure 1 Intraoperative photographs show patient positioning operating room setup for anterior
ankle arthroscopy. A, The patient is placed in the supine position on a flat-top table, and a thigh
tourniquet is applied. The surgical leg is placed in a thigh-support leg holder with padding under
the posterior thigh. The foot should barely touch the table with the knee resting in a flexed
position. B, Necessary surgical tools include a small joint arthroscope and instruments, including
an arthroscope, cannula, 22-gauge spinal needle, and probe. C, After the patient is prepared, a
sterile, noninvasive distractor is placed over the dorsal midfoot and around the posterior heel
and tensioned to bring the ankle into a plantarflexed position. (Reproduced from Digiovanni BF,
Kohring JM: Arthroscopy of the ankle, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic
Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 1157-1166.)
Noninvasive ankle distraction system
Different systems are available. The author of this lesson prefer a noninvasive ankle strap
and distractor2 (Figure 1, C).
The aim is to place the ankle in distraction and in a plantarflexed position to allow for
improved access to the mid and posterior talar dome lesions as necessary and attempt to
avoid malleolar osteotomies if possible. Gross and then fine distraction is applied to a point

the ankle during the procedure.

Soft-tissue ankle impingement
Bony ankle impingement3 (Video 2)
Osteochondral lesions4 (Video 3)
Syndesmotic impingement

Indications
The choice of arthroscopy or an open technique to address ankle pathology depends on
the type and location of pathology and the corrective procedure necessary. Ankle
arthroscopy may be a valuable surgical technique for accessing and addressing certain
intra-articular pathologies with minimal incisions. In addition, ankle arthroscopy can
provide increased visualization for certain pathologies that may be more difficult to
visualize via open techniques or that may otherwise require a bony osteotomy to access.
Certain pathologies lend themselves well to ankle arthroscopy.
Techniques
Portal placement
Anteromedial portal
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:20 AM
AAOS | Ankle Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004080
5/17

The anteromedial portal is placed just medial to the tibialis anterior tendon, at the lateral
tip of the medial malleolus2 (Figure 2).
Injection of the ankle joint with saline, using a 22-gauge spinal needle, helps identify the
correct portal location and distends the joint to facilitate placement of the arthroscope.
The most common error with anteromedial portal location is placement too far medially. If
this occurs, the medial malleolus blocks full manipulation of the arthroscope and
compromises joint visualization.
The structures that are most at risk during anteromedial portal placement are the greater
saphenous nerve and the saphenous vein. A small hemostat is used to bluntly dissect soft
tissue at the portal site in a transverse and longitudinal direction to mobilize the structures
and to allow for free passage of instruments without entrapping neurovascular structures.
Figure 2 Intraoperative photograph of an ankle shows the location of the anteromedial ankle
portal (arrow) for anterior ankle arthroscopy. Note that portal placement is a fair distance away
from the medial malleolus and close to the medial course of the tibialis anterior tendon. This
position ensures that visualization is not obscured by the medial malleolus. (Reproduced from
Digiovanni BF, Kohring JM: Arthroscopy of the ankle, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive
Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp
1157-1166.)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:20 AM
AAOS | Ankle Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004080
6/17

Anterolateral portal
The anterolateral portal is placed at the level of the ankle joint, medial to the lateral
malleolus and in the soft spot just lateral to the peroneus tertius tendon2 (Figure 3).
The anterolateral portal is made under direct visualization with the arthroscope in the
anteromedial portal. A 22-gauge needle aids in atraumatic identification of an appropriate
position parallel to the tibiotalar joint surface and is used as a temporary outflow.
The most common error with anterolateral portal location is placement too far distally. The
portal should be located approximately 5 to 10 mm proximal to the anteromedial portal
site.
The structure that is at greatest risk during placement of the anterolateral portal is the
intermediate dorsal cutaneous branch of the superficial peroneal nerve5 (Figure 4).
Transillumination of the anterolateral skin using the arthroscope can help to identify the
crossing nerve branches.
Blunt dissection with a hemostat is used in the portal incision to keep the nerve branch
from being injured during portal placement and avoid being entrapped during instrument
passage2 (Figure 5).

Figure 5 Arthroscopic images of an ankle shows the normal anatomy the medial tibiotalar joint
viewed from the anterolateral portal (A) and the lateral (B) aspect of the tibiotalar joint (B), at
which the fibula and syndesmotic ligaments can be visualized. (Reproduced from Digiovanni BF,
Kohring JM: Arthroscopy of the ankle, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic

Posterolateral portal
The posterolateral portal is optional and is used for improved visualization of the posterior
third of the tibiotalar joint not fully visualized from the anterior portals.
The posterolateral portal is placed 2 cm proximal to the tip of the lateral malleolus, medial
to the peroneal tendons, and lateral to the Achilles tendon.
A 22-gauge needle can be used to identify the correct location while using the arthroscope
in the anteromedial portal for visualization. Another option is to place a switching stick (a
smooth metal rod) from the anteromedial portal. The switching stick is inserted through
the capsule, and the cannula is placed over the rod through the posterolateral portal.
The most common error with posterolateral portal location is placement too far distally,
which obscures visualization.
The structures that are at greatest risk during placement of the posterolateral portal are
the sural nerve and the lesser saphenous vein.
Preoperative Planning
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:20 AM
AAOS | Ankle Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004080
10/17

Preoperative imaging studies, including radiographs and advanced imaging studies, including
CT scans or MRI, depending on symptoms and pathology, should be thoroughly reviewed to
aid in guiding the arthroscopic correction.
Patient Positioning
Setup/patient positioning
Appropriate patient positioning, the use of a small joint arthroscope, small joint arthroscopic
instruments, and noninvasive distraction are keys to efficient and successful ankle
arthroscopic procedures.
The patient is placed supine on a flat-top operating table. If the patient is taller than 6 feet, a
table extension may be added to the foot of the table to allow noninvasive distraction to be
applied to table.
The thigh leg support is used, with care taken to keep the popliteal fossa free of pressure
and attached to the table at the level of midthigh. A thigh tourniquet typically is used;
however, a sterile pneumatic calf tourniquet may be used for large legs. The heel should rest
just off the bed2 (Figure 1, A).
A hip bump or kidney rest also may be necessary to help internally rotate the leg.
Complications
Many potential complications are possible with ankle arthroscopy. Most complications can be
avoided if the surgeon becomes familiar with the surface anatomy of the region, uses small
joint instruments, and incorporates contemporary noninvasive distraction techniques.
Complications occur in approximately 5% to 7% of patients.
The most common complication is neurologic injury (approximately 80%), with one-half of
those involving the superficial peroneal nerve and one-half possibly related to the
distraction.
Limit the amount of time the ankle is distracted to decrease the risk of nerve irritation.
A synovial cutaneous fistula is more common with ankle arthroscopy than with arthroscopy
of other joints. A short period of immobilization (5 to 7 days) is recommended to decrease
the incidence of draining fistula formation.
Posterior Ankle Arthroscopy
SEND FEEDBACK

11/17

Overview
Posterior ankle arthroscopy provides access to at least 50% of the posterior talar dome and
allows for management of various posterior ankle and hindfoot disorders, both intra-and
extra-articular in nature. These conditions include a symptomatic os trigonum, a prominent
posterior talar process, and a posterior process fracture6 (Video 4).
The patient is placed in a prone position. The use of a soft-tissue distraction device or
tensioned wire placed through the calcaneus may aid in joint visualization2 (Figure 6).
Fluoroscopy may be helpful when making the portals to visualize the direction of
instrumentation.
Video 4 Wiegerinck JI, de Leeuw PAJ, Van Dijk CN: Posterior ankle arthroscopy: Impingement, os
trigonum, FHL tenosynovitis, in Stone JW, Van Dijk CN, eds: The Master’s Experience: Arthroscopic
Surgical Techniques. Advanced Ankle Arthroscopy [DVD]. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2011

Figure 6 Intraoperative photograph of a right ankle shows posterior arthroscopy. A smooth
Steinmann pin is passed from medial to lateral across the calcaneal tuberosity. A single sterile roll
of Kerlix gauze (CardinalHealth) is wrapped around the medial and lateral sides of the pin at the
midportion of the Kerlix roll. The slack from the medial and lateral sides is then passed behind
the surgeon to a nonsterile surgical assistant. The nonsterile surgical assistant then ties the Kerlix
gauze snugly behind the surgeon (behind the surgeon is no longer sterile). The surgeon can lean
back on the Kerlix “belt” to create traction at the ankle. After arthroscopy is complete, a sterile
scissors cuts the sterile end of the Kerlix gauze wrap from the medial and lateral sides of the
calcaneus. The Steinmann pin is removed. (Reproduced from Digiovanni BF, Kohring JM:
Arthroscopy of the ankle, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3.
Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 1157-1166.)
Indications
Posterior ankle impingement, os trigonum syndrome, stenosing tenosynovitis of the flexor
hallucis longus

Techniques
Portal placement
Posterolateral portal
The posterolateral portal is made adjacent to the Achilles tendon just above the level of the
lateral malleolus. Direct a clamp anteriorly in the direction of the first webspace until it hits
the tibia. Use this same path when inserting the arthroscope.
The incision should only be made through the skin; then use blunt dissection to avoid
injuring the sural nerve.
Posteromedial portal
The posteromedial portal is made at the same level as the posterolateral portal just above
the tip of the medial malleolus. An incision is made on the medial aspect of the Achilles
tendon. It may be helpful to use a clamp to make this portal before inserting instruments.
Orient the clamp toward the arthroscope at a 90° angle, aiming in the direction of the third
webspace. After the clamp touches the arthroscope, redirect it anteriorly toward the ankle
joint until it reaches bone.
The flexor hallucis longus is the key landmark for posterior ankle arthroscopy2 (Figure 7).
Instruments should always remain lateral to this structure to avoid the neurovascular
bundle, including the tibial nerve and the posterior tibial artery and veins.
Figure 7 Arthroscopic image of a left ankle shows posterior arthroscopy. An arthroscopic shaver
has exposed the flexor hallucis longus muscle at the posteromedial aspect of the ankle. The
flexor hallucis longus should be the medial-most extent of posterior ankle débridement. Any
débridement more medial than the flexor hallucis longus should be performed judiciously, with
concern for injury to the neurovascular bundle. (Reproduced from Digiovanni BF, Kohring JM:

Arthroscopy of the ankle, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3.
Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 1157-1166.)
Preoperative Planning
Surgeons should be prepared for the necessity of a small open procedure if the bone not able
to be fully resected via the arthroscopy portals. Surgeons also should have a fluoroscopic
imaging unit (C-arm or mini C-arm) available to evaluate the resection on completion.
Patient Positioning
Setup/patient positioning
The patient is placed in the prone position for better access.
The use of a soft-tissue distraction device or tensioned wire placed through the calcaneus
may aid in joint visualization.
Fluoroscopy
Fluoroscopy may be helpful in making the portals to visualize the direction of
instrumentation and for portal placement.
Postoperative protocol
Early movement and weight bearing are encouraged after wound healing has occurred to
prevent the formation of scar tissue and preserve range of motion.
Complications

Complications
Nerve injuries are the most common complications and occur in approximately 4% of
patients. They may include injuries to the tibial or sural nerve, resulting in loss of
sensation to the plantar or lateral foot or nerve pain.
